cards.title: Diagnose bottom-of-funnel objections before writing BOF creative
cards.summary: Segment non-buyers into price, trust, quality and timing objections, then match each to a specific bottom-of-funnel creative treatment.
cards.use_when: Planning retargeting and bottom-of-funnel ad creative for shoppers who visited the store or PDP but did not purchase.
steps: Recognize the BOF audience is a mix: the source estimates roughly one group objecting to price, another doubting trust/quality, and roughly 20% who simply aren't ready yet (too soon, first touch).
For price objections: run discount-led creative, value anchoring, and cost-per-use framing — e.g. compare a supplement to coffee ('half the price of a coffee with the same caffeine').
For trust objections: lead with social proof — customer counts, number of five-star reviews, UGC testimonials.
For quality/product doubt: show UGC of the product in use, before/afters, and demonstrations.
For 'too soon' buyers: stay present with educational or lifestyle content rather than hard sell.
Build your BOF asset mix in these proportions so each objection is handled somewhere in the retargeting set.
caveats: The objection-mix percentages are the source's estimate, not measured data from your account.
Creative treatments are not quantified here; test treatments against each other rather than assuming one wins.

cards.title: Creative volume hierarchy: volume beats concept, hook and editing
cards.summary: Rank creative production priorities as volume, concept quality, hook strength, editing, UGC talent, storytelling — and target a minimum quality bar rather than guessing winners.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest limited ad-production effort and headcount across hooks, concepts, editing and creators.
steps: Order effort by the source's hierarchy: 1) volume, 2) concept quality, 3) hook strength, 4) editing quality, 5) UGC talent, 6) storytelling.
Accept the source's claim that even top creative strategists cannot reliably pick which of several objectively good ads will win — prediction at the top end is essentially guessing.
Instead of predicting winners, define a minimum 'bar of quality' (the source's example bar is roughly 7/10) that an ad must clear.
Produce as much volume as possible that clears the bar; once above the bar, ads are effectively indistinguishable in predicted performance.

Audit your account if you are pushing high volume: check whether added ads actually contain good concepts, hooks and awareness-stage-appropriate formats — otherwise it is 'junk volume' that clears volume but not the bar.
caveats: The 7/10 bar is an illustrative standard from the source, not a measured threshold.
The 'volume first' ranking is the presenter's opinion and assumes the quality bar is already defined internally.

cards.title: Calculate creative volume from spend or from hit-rate back-propagation
cards.summary: Use $1,000 monthly ad spend per new ad as a quick rule, or back-propagate required volume from average spend per ad, expected revenue and new-customer revenue targets.
cards.use_when: Setting how many new creatives to brief per month for a given ad budget or new-customer revenue target.
steps: Quick rule: one new ad per $1,000 of monthly ad spend — e.g. $30K/month = 30 new ads, $50K/month = 50 new ads. The source states this applies roughly in AUD and translates similarly to USD.
Better method: calculate average spend per ad from historical data. Example — 500 ads launched over a year with $500K spent = $1,000 average spend per ad.

Determine average return per ad using acquisition MER (new customer revenue ÷ ad spend) or blended ROAS, measured on a 7-day-click basis. Example — $1,000 mean spend × 3 ROAS = $3,000 expected revenue per ad.
Back-propagate from targets: $300K monthly new-customer revenue ÷ $3,000 expected revenue per ad = 100 creatives per month required.
Flex creative volume as your revenue forecast changes through the year so creative volume tracks expected new-customer revenue.
Forecast winners and losers separately and add the average time-lag before an ad's revenue lands — the simple model ignores both.
caveats: The $1,000-per-ad and 7-day-click conventions are source-specific heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
The simple formula assumes equal ad outcomes; if a month is all losers or all winners, actual revenue diverges sharply.

cards.title: Set the creative production budget as a share of media spend by scale
cards.summary: Allocate 0% cash (founder time) at 4–30K/month, 25% of media budget to production at 30–100K/month, and ~10% above 100K/month.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget to put into creative production versus ad distribution at your current monthly spend level.
steps: At $4K–$30K/month spend: keep content founder-led. The source argues production budget should be your time, not money — statics and founder-led iPhone videos can carry spend to $30K/month. Founder involvement also builds the internal standard for what good creative looks like so you can later train and KPI others.

At $30K–$100K/month: allocate 25% of media budget to production (e.g. $25K/month at $100K spend). The source deliberately calls this uncomfortable but argues most brands under-spend here and that's why they stall.
Above $100K/month: let production asymptote toward ~10% of media budget. At a 25% MER, 10% of media budget equals roughly 2.5% of total revenue.
Budgets at the 25% level are intended to fund UGC, partnership ads, a designer on statics (full-time international or part-time in-house) and possibly a low-cost agency supplement (e.g. VSLs).
caveats: Percentages are the source's recommended allocations, not industry benchmarks; validate against your own contribution margins.
The source presents the 25% mid-band as intentionally uncomfortable and notes it 'democratizes' at scale — treat as a directional target, not a hard rule.

cards.title: Treat creative as a revenue driver, not a cost centre: the redistribution math
cards.summary: Model the efficiency gain from moving ad budget into production versus running too few ads, and avoid the failure mode of scaling a starved account.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shift spend from distribution channels into creative production when the account has few active ads relative to spend.
steps: Check your active-ad count against spend. The source's case example: a brand spending $350K/month on Meta had only ~15 live ads, an extreme mismatch.
When active ads are too few, media buyers over-compensate with account mechanics (over-segmentation, 25 campaigns, cost caps) because creative is the actual bottleneck.

Build the reallocation case explicitly: the source proposed moving $10K/month from Meta to production, which with an agency would yield ~40 assets (mix of unique, hook-swaps and statics), nearly doubling active ads and likely unlocking ~5% efficiency.

Translate the efficiency gain two ways: a 5% efficiency improvement on $350K = ~$17.5K saved (drop $10K spend, net ~$7.5K better), or hold spend flat and gain incremental revenue at their ~3x return (~$40–50K/month extra).
Treat creative budget as comparable to reallocating between channels — a distribution decision, not purely a cost line.
If you keep allocating nothing to production, expect the account to fatigue back down: this source reports the example brand's performance decayed as its 60 ads fatigued and spend reallocated away.
caveats: All figures are from a single client example and are illustrative, not a promised result.
The source states the brand eventually parted ways with the agency; this is a cautionary case, not a controlled test.

cards.title: Test creative volume cheaply with trial reels before ad manager
cards.summary: Post ad cutdowns as trial reels with the CTA removed to get view data and retention graphs, then only push the best hooks into the ad account.
cards.use_when: Choosing which hooks or early-cut creative to fund with paid spend, or iterating on a video before final production.
steps: Export the ad asset and cut off the end call-to-action, then post it as a trial reel on the brand or personal page. The source states this applied as of April 2026.
Use the two outputs: (1) comparative virality/view data across posts, and (2) retention graphs showing where viewers drop.
Read the retention graph to diagnose whether the hook, bridge or body is losing viewers, and iterate on the next shoot accordingly.
Run V1 as a trial reel while round two is still in production so feedback arrives within ~24 hours, before the final asset is finished.
For hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, identify the strongest, and push only ~5 into the ad account rather than spending media budget discovering the same thing.
caveats: The source explicitly flags this as a time-sensitive tactic that may change as algorithms change — verify current trial reel behavior before relying on it.
Trial reels measure organic virality and retention, not purchase conversion or ROAS.

cards.title: Understand creative fatigue as spend capacity plus audience size
cards.summary: Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; fatigue comes from either the asset going stale or the targeted audience being too small.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to push a winning ad harder, introduce replacements, or re-target a narrow persona.
steps: Model each ad's life: spend ramps (manually or via Meta distribution), hits a maximum daily spend limit, then decays and is eventually turned off or stops receiving spend. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.
Accept two premises: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and be turned off.

Choose a shape deliberately: squeeze spend hard for short-term sell-through (higher peak, faster falloff) versus hold at a lower daily budget so the ad lives 6 months instead of 6 weeks (portfolio management view).

Tie the choice to inventory and cash: if you must clear inventory this month, squeezing a winner to sell through may be right even at degraded MER; if inventory is tight or you're growing faster than your cash conversion cycle, let ads breathe for higher efficiency.

Diagnose fatigue cause: (1) the ad is stale or repeats visuals/concepts/audience of other creatives — this fatigues faster when value propositions repeat; (2) the persona is too small, so frequency rises and profitability falls.
For narrow personas, rotate creative within the audience and account for churn (e.g. marathon-training audiences continually refresh), but do not over-saturate.
caveats: The source notes agencies without business context tend to squeeze winners for a 30–90 day case study and short-term ROAS, damaging long-term account health.
Spend-capacity is a conceptual model, not a precise measurable figure.

cards.title: Match persona breadth to spend capacity; go specific first, broad later
cards.summary: Narrow persona callouts cap daily spend capacity; broader audiences scale further but demand stronger creative — start specific, expand at scale.
cards.use_when: Choosing how specific the persona callout in an ad script should be, or deciding when to broaden targeting to scale spend.
steps: Recognize that narrower callouts cap daily spend: the source's example of 'e-commerce CFOs in Australia owning over $100M' is a pool of roughly 1,000–2,000 people — spending $10K/day would hit them absurdly often.
Broaden the callout to scale: 'e-commerce founders earning over $100K/year' is a much larger pool and supports far higher daily spend.
Exploit audience churn: people enter and exit a specific persona (e.g. new marathon entrants), so rotate creatives to reach new entrants at a sustainable frequency rather than oversaturating.
Prefer specific callouts at first because they force sharper, better creative that resonates; only move to broader audiences once you reach scale, even though broad audiences spend further.

For ecommerce application: a tight callout like 'runners chasing a sub-4 marathon' may only support a few hundred dollars/day, whereas a broader 'runners' angle supports much more — but the specific version often converts better per impression.
caveats: The source notes high-quality top-of-funnel unaware creative is very difficult and says most brands should not attempt it unless they are already a $50M+ brand.
Broad callouts do not automatically outperform; they require creative that resonates with more people.

cards.title: Recover spend from fatiguing ads with four tactics
cards.summary: Iterate hooks, move ads to cost-cap campaigns, re-use post IDs in scaling campaigns, or translate formats to extract more spend from a decaying winner.
cards.use_when: Extending a winning ad's life before turning it off or replacing it.
steps: Iterate the asset: take a proven hero ad and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same body.
Move the ad into a cost-cap campaign to force more spend through it — a short-term media-buying tactic that also accelerates fatigue.
Carry the creative into another campaign (e.g. a scaling campaign) using the post ID so existing engagement is retained; the source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.
Translate formats: video → static, VSSL → UGC, static → long-form-copy unaware static. This is a variation on iteration and often the most durable option.
Accept that once a creative has fatigued there is limited upside; these tactics squeeze the back end. The real answer is a portfolio of other well-performing ads to fall back on.
caveats: Duplicating adsets is named but the source does not recommend it, calling it a dated tactic.
Cost-cap moves and post-ID re-use are explicitly described as tactical, not business-changing.

cards.title: Run portfolio management across ads, products and the balance sheet
cards.summary: Above ~$50K/month, treat media buying as risk diversification across ads and products, and reconcile P&L optimisation with balance-sheet/inventory reality.
cards.use_when: Setting media buying priorities when running a large ad account, especially if unsold inventory is accumulating or efficiency targets conflict with sell-through.
steps: Apply the 80/20 pattern deliberately: decide whether you want Pareto concentration to occur naturally in the account or introduce structure to avoid over-leverage on a few ads.
Apply the same logic to products so spend is not over-concentrated on a small number of SKUs.
Recognise agencies are KPI'd on efficiency and profit, so they optimise toward maximum profit — that can under-optimise the balance sheet.
Check for the failure case: a business showing $2M P&L profit but holding $3M in unsold inventory is effectively negative $1M in cash.
If stuck with unsold stock, restructure the account to sell it through, accepting lower efficiency and making creatives for that stock — the source calls this a hard pill but the way out.
Keep the media buyer across inventory position so spend decisions align with stock reality.
caveats: The $50K/month threshold is the source's stated point at which this becomes the media buyer's job.
Profit-vs-balance-sheet framing is the presenter's opinion about agency incentives, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Budget creative effort across replication, iteration and net-new
cards.summary: Allocate roughly 50–60% to replicating winners, 20–30% to iterating underperformers, and 20–30% to net-new concepts — most brands over-weight net-new.
cards.use_when: Planning a monthly creative production calendar and deciding which types of assets to brief.
steps: Categorise every asset into one of three types, prioritised by leverage: (1) winning content replication — re-making winners via hook iterations or format translations; (2) iterative content — fixing underperformers via hook/format changes, new personas or new offers; (3) net-new concepts — entirely new formats, angles and ideas.
Apply the source's recommended split: ~50–60% winning replication, ~20–30% iteration, ~20–30% net-new. The exact split shifts with business context.
Do not skip net-new entirely (some brands run 0%) — everything fatigues, so a pipeline of new concepts is required to feed the top of the system.
Avoid over-weighting net-new: the source admits doing 80–90% net-new in his own organic content and reports replication held ~80% of views while net-new underperformed.
Re-post and re-make content that worked instead of only creating new: each re-run reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly.
caveats: Percentages are the source's general recommendation and are explicitly context-dependent.
The 80% view-share observation is from the presenter's own organic content, not a controlled ecommerce test.

cards.title: Brief creators with their past work plus the brief behind it
cards.summary: Creator output quality follows brief quality; assess a creator by comparing what they produced against the brief they were given.
cards.use_when: Sourcing and briefing UGC creators or agencies for ecommerce ad production.
steps: Ask for examples of past work — the source calls skipping this self-evidently wrong.
For each example, request the original brief that the creator was given, so you can compare output to brief one-for-one.
Read the comparison: if they produced something great from a terrible brief, you can give them broad strokes; if the brief was extremely detailed, match that level in your own brief.
Default to writing the highest-quality, most in-depth brief possible.
If a creator doesn't want to follow the script, ask for one scripted take and one natural take, then choose or run both.

Ensure the creator is native to the target region: the source reports Australian accents underperform in the US, native US accents are needed, and UK-to-AU translates decently — but native accents always outperform. The script can be identical; the creator must be local.
caveats: Region-accuracy claims are the presenter's reported observation, not a benchmarked study.

cards.title: Build the creative production team by spend tier
cards.summary: Hire a video editor, static designer and creative strategist (plus creators) in a tiered structure matched to monthly ad spend.
cards.use_when: Planning creative production headcount and roles for an ecommerce ad account as spend scales.
steps: At $4–30K/month: founder creates content (iPhone quality is fine, natural feel matters), scripts are where leverage lives, run ~3 core concepts, and allocate 60–80% of budget to testing since there isn't enough spend to scale winners.
At $30–100K/month: two to three UGC creators, ~5–6 concepts, a testing and a scaling campaign, ~30–100 new creatives per month, and introduce partnership ads.

Above $100K/month: a full team — scripter, editor, designer, and 4–6 creators (may be part-time), at least 10% of budget to creative, 8–10 active concepts, 100+ new assets/month, plus a financial model tracking cost per asset by source and profit contribution per ad, and ROI per ad against production cost.

Hire the roles as: a video editor (ideally AI-native for more assets and synthetic footage), a static designer, and a creative strategist. Both editor and designer can be global, part-time contractors or full-time.

Source the strategist role from copywriters (strategy is mostly copywriting — scripts, static briefs, persona ideation), by poaching from another company, or by backfilling a designer/editor into the role (faster feedback loops).
Optionally pay the strategist a variable tied to ad spend for their creatives — the source cites ~3% of ad spend working well mid-size but becoming absurd at large scale (e.g. $80K/month).
caveats: Tier thresholds and headcount are the source's recommendations, not universal requirements.
The ~3% ad-spend incentive model is the source's observation; he explicitly notes it breaks at large scale.

cards.title: Automate the middle of the creative process with AI, not the ends
cards.summary: Apply AI heavily to briefing and script writing and to production, but not to ideation or final analysis.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to insert LLM/AI tooling into your creative production workflow.
steps: Map the process: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis → back to ideation.
Do not automate ideation: the source states LLMs output the meme, and no amount of context or scraping produces sufficiently differentiated ideas — a strategist must validate concepting.

Heavily automate briefing and script writing: build a Claude skill that walks through a ~20-question questionnaire (persona, concept, offer, long-form or not, stage of awareness) and outputs a script/brief that is ~99% done with a ~1% tweak.
Leverage AI in production: it speeds workflows, and the source reports VSSLs and static image ads can be ~90% AI-produced.
Use AI with caution in analysis: it does not naturally weight your metric hierarchy or account structure context; the source reports AI analysis often misleads core decisions.
Net rule: skip the outsides of the process (ideation, final analysis), maximise throughput in the middle (briefing, production).
caveats: The '99% done' and '90% AI' figures are the source's estimates, not measured outcomes.
Tool names and interfaces may change — verify current capabilities of your AI tooling.

cards.title: Match persona callouts and creative to audience warmth and account scale
cards.summary: Use broad audience creative only if you can sustain it; start content-first and video-heavy, and match creative to the awareness stage.
cards.use_when: Setting the targeting and creative approach for a new or growing ecommerce brand.
steps: For a smaller founder: post organically every day before going paid. The source argues this is the right approach for 2026–27 not because organic outperforms paid, but because it forces you to get good at creative that compounds into ads.
Diagnose your creative using retention graphs, shares and saves — the same signals that tell you whether an ad holds attention.
Recognise top-of-funnel unaware advertising has a very high skill ceiling; the source says most shouldn't attempt it unless already a $50M+ brand.
Use specific persona callouts that force sharper creative first, and only broaden once you have the scale to justify it.
Be careful with DPAs: the source warns they are generally good but tend to over-spend and their ROAS is over-inflated.
caveats: The '$50M+ brand' qualifier is the source's opinion.
DPA over-spend is the presenter's observation, not a benchmark; test incrementality on your own account.

cards.title: Google Ads structure: consolidation beats segmentation, unless commercial reality forces segmentation
cards.summary: Merge low-data campaigns into consolidated ones so the algorithm learns from more conversions, and only split out for commercial necessity (clearance, new arrivals).
cards.use_when: Restructuring an ecommerce Google Ads account that is fragmented into many campaigns with low conversion volumes.
steps: Understand the rule: campaigns learn in isolation — a campaign with 50 monthly conversions optimises from 50 data points, while a sibling with 10 optimises from 10 (ignore limited platform-level sharing for the model).
Expect the pattern: as conversion volume per campaign falls, ROAS tends to fall with it, usually causally.

Fix by consolidating: delete the low-volume campaigns and move their products and budget into the highest-conversion campaign so all conversions train one model (e.g. 90 conversions/month instead of 50+20+10).
Segment only when a commercial reality demands it — the source's examples: grade-C inventory you must burn or discount, and new arrivals that need shopping visibility for seasonality.
Key principle: be as consolidated as possible while injecting only the commercial realities that justify a split.
caveats: The 'consolidation beats segmentation' rule applies to Google Ads campaign structure as the source describes it; verify against your current account setup.
The 50/20/10 conversion example is illustrative, not a measured result.

cards.title: Recognise Google spend as either over-spending or under-spending
cards.summary: Google sits bottom-of-funnel and captures existing demand at high ROAS, which leads to two opposite errors: pushing spend that isn't incremental, or refusing to scale when cold search demand exists.
cards.use_when: Auditing Google Ads spend levels and deciding whether to increase, hold or decrease budget.
steps: Overspend pattern: top-of-funnel demand is generated by Meta/TikTok/affiliates, and Google captures the bottom intent and claims high ROAS. Brands push spend up on Google even though it isn't incremental, and end up over-spending.

Underspend pattern: brands that believe Google is only bottom-funnel refuse to spend above ~$10K/month even while spending $4M/month on Meta — despite having scalable cold search demand in their category.
Decide which camp you are in and move spend accordingly.
Test incrementality rather than trusting platform ROAS alone — the source's own test was finding PMAX reported a 5 ROAS while backend revenue didn't move when budget doubled.
Use the platform's reported ROAS as a hypothesis, and hold-out or incrementality testing as the check.
caveats: The $10K/month and $4M/month figures are the source's example, not a threshold.
Incrementality testing methodology is not detailed here; treat the platform ROAS as unverified for causal claims.

cards.title: Apply the five major Google Ads shifts when restructuring in 2026
cards.summary: Account for PMAX's ceiling, standard shopping's return, changed match-type definitions, AIMAX/demand gen, and DSA deprecation before rebuilding the account.
cards.use_when: Revisiting a Google Ads account built on older playbooks or when PMAX stops scaling.
steps: PMAX has hit its ceiling: early discounts in the auction created arbitrage, then everyone moved spend in and the advantage went away. There's no clear visibility into where spend goes, and scaling PMAX to $100–300K/month did not produce matching backend revenue in the source's tests.
Standard shopping is back: once PMAX scales far enough it shows diminishing returns, and layering standard shopping is required to keep growing cold new-customer acquisition.

Match types changed: exact match now matches on meaning, phrase match broadened, broad match stayed broad. SCAGs (single-keyword ad groups) is no longer recommended — the source says it stopped working around 2020.
AIMAX and demand gen have been introduced; DSAs are being deprecated.
Structure the account around these realities rather than 2022–23 playbooks, and expect the platform to ship changes every few months.
caveats: This reflects the source's 2026 view; verify current platform behaviour and product availability before acting.

The source states this applied as of April 2026.","Use the two outputs: (1) comparative virality/view data across posts, and (2) retention graphs showing where viewers drop.","Read the retention graph to diagnose whether the hook, bridge or body is losing viewers, and iterate on the next shoot accordingly.","Run V1 as a trial reel while round two is still in production so feedback arrives within ~24 hours, before the final asset is finished.","For hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, identify the strongest, and push only ~5 into the ad account rather than spending media budget discovering the same thing."],"caveats":["The source explicitly flags this as a time-sensitive tactic that may change as algorithms change — verify current trial reel behavior before relying on it.","Trial reels measure organic virality and retention, not purchase conversion or ROAS."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","experiment-design","acquisition","hook-testing","trial-reels"]},{"title":"Understand creative fatigue as spend capacity plus audience size","summary":"Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; fatigue comes from either the asset going stale or the targeted audience being too small.","use_when":"Deciding whether to push a winning ad harder, introduce replacements, or re-target a narrow persona.","steps":["Model each ad's life: spend ramps (manually or via Meta distribution), hits a maximum daily spend limit, then decays and is eventually turned off or stops receiving spend. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.","Accept two premises: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and be turned off.","Choose a shape deliberately: squeeze spend hard for short-term sell-through (higher peak, faster falloff) versus hold at a lower daily budget so the ad lives 6 months instead of 6 weeks (portfolio management view).","Tie the choice to inventory and cash: if you must clear inventory this month, squeezing a winner to sell through may be right even at degraded MER; if inventory is tight or you're growing faster than your cash conversion cycle, let ads breathe for higher efficiency.","Diagnose fatigue cause: (1) the ad is stale or repeats visuals/concepts/audience of other creatives — this fatigues faster when value propositions repeat; (2) the persona is too small, so frequency rises and profitability falls.","For narrow personas, rotate creative within the audience and account for churn (e.g. marathon-training audiences continually refresh), but do not over-saturate."],"caveats":["The source notes agencies without business context tend to squeeze winners for a 30–90 day case study and short-term ROAS, damaging long-term account health.","Spend-capacity is a conceptual model, not a precise measurable figure."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","media-buying","inventory","acquisition","frequency"]},{"title":"Match persona breadth to spend capacity; go specific first, broad later","summary":"Narrow persona callouts cap daily spend capacity; broader audiences scale further but demand stronger creative — start specific, expand at scale.","use_when":"Choosing how specific the persona callout in an ad script should be, or deciding when to broaden targeting to scale spend.","steps":["Recognize that narrower callouts cap daily spend: the source's example of 'e-commerce CFOs in Australia owning over $100M' is a pool of roughly 1,000–2,000 people — spending $10K/day would hit them absurdly often.","Broaden the callout to scale: 'e-commerce founders earning over $100K/year' is a much larger pool and supports far higher daily spend.","Exploit audience churn: people enter and exit a specific persona (e.g. new marathon entrants), so rotate creatives to reach new entrants at a sustainable frequency rather than oversaturating.","Prefer specific callouts at first because they force sharper, better creative that resonates; only move to broader audiences once you reach scale, even though broad audiences spend further.","For ecommerce application: a tight callout like 'runners chasing a sub-4 marathon' may only support a few hundred dollars/day, whereas a broader 'runners' angle supports much more — but the specific version often converts better per impression."],"caveats":["The source notes high-quality top-of-funnel unaware creative is very difficult and says most brands should not attempt it unless they are already a $50M+ brand.","Broad callouts do not automatically outperform; they require creative that resonates with more people."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","targeting","audience-research","acquisition","personas"]},{"title":"Recover spend from fatiguing ads with four tactics","summary":"Iterate hooks, move ads to cost-cap campaigns, re-use post IDs in scaling campaigns, or translate formats to extract more spend from a decaying winner.","use_when":"Extending a winning ad's life before turning it off or replacing it.","steps":["Iterate the asset: take a proven hero ad and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same body.","Move the ad into a cost-cap campaign to force more spend through it — a short-term media-buying tactic that also accelerates fatigue.","Carry the creative into another campaign (e.g. a scaling campaign) using the post ID so existing engagement is retained; the source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.","Translate formats: video → static, VSSL → UGC, static → long-form-copy unaware static. This is a variation on iteration and often the most durable option.","Accept that once a creative has fatigued there is limited upside; these tactics squeeze the back end. The real answer is a portfolio of other well-performing ads to fall back on."],"caveats":["Duplicating adsets is named but the source does not recommend it, calling it a dated tactic.","Cost-cap moves and post-ID re-use are explicitly described as tactical, not business-changing."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","media-buying","experiment-design","ad-iteration","scaling"]},{"title":"Run portfolio management across ads, products and the balance sheet","summary":"Above ~$50K/month, treat media buying as risk diversification across ads and products, and reconcile P&L optimisation with balance-sheet/inventory reality.","use_when":"Setting media buying priorities when running a large ad account, especially if unsold inventory is accumulating or efficiency targets conflict with sell-through.","steps":["Apply the 80/20 pattern deliberately: decide whether you want Pareto concentration to occur naturally in the account or introduce structure to avoid over-leverage on a few ads.","Apply the same logic to products so spend is not over-concentrated on a small number of SKUs.","Recognise agencies are KPI'd on efficiency and profit, so they optimise toward maximum profit — that can under-optimise the balance sheet.","Check for the failure case: a business showing $2M P&L profit but holding $3M in unsold inventory is effectively negative $1M in cash.","If stuck with unsold stock, restructure the account to sell it through, accepting lower efficiency and making creatives for that stock — the source calls this a hard pill but the way out.","Keep the media buyer across inventory position so spend decisions align with stock reality."],"caveats":["The $50K/month threshold is the source's stated point at which this becomes the media buyer's job.","Profit-vs-balance-sheet framing is the presenter's opinion about agency incentives, not a universal rule."],"tags":["multi","inventory","media-buying","measurement","cash-flow","merchandising"]},{"title":"Budget creative effort across replication, iteration and net-new","summary":"Allocate roughly 50–60% to replicating winners, 20–30% to iterating underperformers, and 20–30% to net-new concepts — most brands over-weight net-new.","use_when":"Planning a monthly creative production calendar and deciding which types of assets to brief.","steps":["Categorise every asset into one of three types, prioritised by leverage: (1) winning content replication — re-making winners via hook iterations or format translations; (2) iterative content — fixing underperformers via hook/format changes, new personas or new offers; (3) net-new concepts — entirely new formats, angles and ideas.","Apply the source's recommended split: ~50–60% winning replication, ~20–30% iteration, ~20–30% net-new. The exact split shifts with business context.","Do not skip net-new entirely (some brands run 0%) — everything fatigues, so a pipeline of new concepts is required to feed the top of the system.","Avoid over-weighting net-new: the source admits doing 80–90% net-new in his own organic content and reports replication held ~80% of views while net-new underperformed.","Re-post and re-make content that worked instead of only creating new: each re-run reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly."],"caveats":["Percentages are the source's general recommendation and are explicitly context-dependent.","The 80% view-share observation is from the presenter's own organic content, not a controlled ecommerce test."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","ad-production","experiment-design","organic-content","iteration"]},{"title":"Brief creators with their past work plus the brief behind it","summary":"Creator output quality follows brief quality; assess a creator by comparing what they produced against the brief they were given.","use_when":"Sourcing and briefing UGC creators or agencies for ecommerce ad production.","steps":["Ask for examples of past work — the source calls skipping this self-evidently wrong.","For each example, request the original brief that the creator was given, so you can compare output to brief one-for-one.","Read the comparison: if they produced something great from a terrible brief, you can give them broad strokes; if the brief was extremely detailed, match that level in your own brief.","Default to writing the highest-quality, most in-depth brief possible.","If a creator doesn't want to follow the script, ask for one scripted take and one natural take, then choose or run both.","Ensure the creator is native to the target region: the source reports Australian accents underperform in the US, native US accents are needed, and UK-to-AU translates decently — but native accents always outperform. The script can be identical; the creator must be local."],"caveats":["Region-accuracy claims are the presenter's reported observation, not a benchmarked study."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","ugc","ad-production","briefing","localisation"]},{"title":"Build the creative production team by spend tier","summary":"Hire a video editor, static designer and creative strategist (plus creators) in a tiered structure matched to monthly ad spend.","use_when":"Planning creative production headcount and roles for an ecommerce ad account as spend scales.","steps":["At $4–30K/month: founder creates content (iPhone quality is fine, natural feel matters), scripts are where leverage lives, run ~3 core concepts, and allocate 60–80% of budget to testing since there isn't enough spend to scale winners.","At $30–100K/month: two to three UGC creators, ~5–6 concepts, a testing and a scaling campaign, ~30–100 new creatives per month, and introduce partnership ads.","Above $100K/month: a full team — scripter, editor, designer, and 4–6 creators (may be part-time), at least 10% of budget to creative, 8–10 active concepts, 100+ new assets/month, plus a financial model tracking cost per asset by source and profit contribution per ad, and ROI per ad against production cost.","Hire the roles as: a video editor (ideally AI-native for more assets and synthetic footage), a static designer, and a creative strategist. Both editor and designer can be global, part-time contractors or full-time.","Source the strategist role from copywriters (strategy is mostly copywriting — scripts, static briefs, persona ideation), by poaching from another company, or by backfilling a designer/editor into the role (faster feedback loops).","Optionally pay the strategist a variable tied to ad spend for their creatives — the source cites ~3% of ad spend working well mid-size but becoming absurd at large scale (e.g. $80K/month)."],"caveats":["Tier thresholds and headcount are the source's recommendations, not universal requirements.","The ~3% ad-spend incentive model is the source's observation; he explicitly notes it breaks at large scale."],"tags":["multi","ad-production","team-structure","creative-strategy","budgeting","hiring"]},{"title":"Automate the middle of the creative process with AI, not the ends","summary":"Apply AI heavily to briefing and script writing and to production, but not to ideation or final analysis.","use_when":"Deciding where to insert LLM/AI tooling into your creative production workflow.","steps":["Map the process: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis → back to ideation.","Do not automate ideation: the source states LLMs output the meme, and no amount of context or scraping produces sufficiently differentiated ideas — a strategist must validate concepting.","Heavily automate briefing and script writing: build a Claude skill that walks through a ~20-question questionnaire (persona, concept, offer, long-form or not, stage of awareness) and outputs a script/brief that is ~99% done with a ~1% tweak.","Leverage AI in production: it speeds workflows, and the source reports VSSLs and static image ads can be ~90% AI-produced.","Use AI with caution in analysis: it does not naturally weight your metric hierarchy or account structure context; the source reports AI analysis often misleads core decisions.","Net rule: skip the outsides of the process (ideation, final analysis), maximise throughput in the middle (briefing, production)."],"caveats":["The '99% done' and '90% AI' figures are the source's estimates, not measured outcomes.","Tool names and interfaces may change — verify current capabilities of your AI tooling."],"tags":["multi","ad-production","ai-tools","creative-strategy","workflow","briefing"]},{"title":"Match persona callouts and creative to audience warmth and account scale","summary":"Use broad audience creative only if you can sustain it; start content-first and video-heavy, and match creative to the awareness stage.","use_when":"Setting the targeting and creative approach for a new or growing ecommerce brand.","steps":["For a smaller founder: post organically every day before going paid. The source argues this is the right approach for 2026–27 not because organic outperforms paid, but because it forces you to get good at creative that compounds into ads.","Diagnose your creative using retention graphs, shares and saves — the same signals that tell you whether an ad holds attention.","Recognise top-of-funnel unaware advertising has a very high skill ceiling; the source says most shouldn't attempt it unless already a $50M+ brand.","Use specific persona callouts that force sharper creative first, and only broaden once you have the scale to justify it.","Be careful with DPAs: the source warns they are generally good but tend to over-spend and their ROAS is over-inflated."],"caveats":["The '$50M+ brand' qualifier is the source's opinion.","DPA over-spend is the presenter's observation, not a benchmark; test incrementality on your own account."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","targeting","organic-content","acquisition","personas"]},{"title":"Google Ads structure: consolidation beats segmentation, unless commercial reality forces segmentation","summary":"Merge low-data campaigns into consolidated ones so the algorithm learns from more conversions, and only split out for commercial necessity (clearance, new arrivals).","use_when":"Restructuring an ecommerce Google Ads account that is fragmented into many campaigns with low conversion volumes.","steps":["Understand the rule: campaigns learn in isolation — a campaign with 50 monthly conversions optimises from 50 data points, while a sibling with 10 optimises from 10 (ignore limited platform-level sharing for the model).","Expect the pattern: as conversion volume per campaign falls, ROAS tends to fall with it, usually causally.","Fix by consolidating: delete the low-volume campaigns and move their products and budget into the highest-conversion campaign so all conversions train one model (e.g. 90 conversions/month instead of 50+20+10).","Segment only when a commercial reality demands it — the source's examples: grade-C inventory you must burn or discount, and new arrivals that need shopping visibility for seasonality.","Key principle: be as consolidated as possible while injecting only the commercial realities that justify a split."],"caveats":["The 'consolidation beats segmentation' rule applies to Google Ads campaign structure as the source describes it; verify against your current account setup.","The 50/20/10 conversion example is illustrative, not a measured result."],"tags":["multi","google-ads","campaign-structure","media-buying","measurement","inventory"]},{"title":"Recognise Google spend as either over-spending or under-spending","summary":"Google sits bottom-of-funnel and captures existing demand at high ROAS, which leads to two opposite errors: pushing spend that isn't incremental, or refusing to scale when cold search demand exists.","use_when":"Auditing Google Ads spend levels and deciding whether to increase, hold or decrease budget.","steps":["Overspend pattern: top-of-funnel demand is generated by Meta/TikTok/affiliates, and Google captures the bottom intent and claims high ROAS. Brands push spend up on Google even though it isn't incremental, and end up over-spending.","Underspend pattern: brands that believe Google is only bottom-funnel refuse to spend above ~$10K/month even while spending $4M/month on Meta — despite having scalable cold search demand in their category.","Decide which camp you are in and move spend accordingly.","Test incrementality rather than trusting platform ROAS alone — the source's own test was finding PMAX reported a 5 ROAS while backend revenue didn't move when budget doubled.","Use the platform's reported ROAS as a hypothesis, and hold-out or incrementality testing as the check."],"caveats":["The $10K/month and $4M/month figures are the source's example, not a threshold.","Incrementality testing methodology is not detailed here; treat the platform ROAS as unverified for causal claims."],"tags":["multi","google-ads","measurement","incrementality","acquisition","budgeting"]},{"title":"Apply the five major Google Ads shifts when restructuring in 2026","summary":"Account for PMAX's ceiling, standard shopping's return, changed match-type definitions, AIMAX/demand gen, and DSA deprecation before rebuilding the account.","use_when":"Revisiting a Google Ads account built on older playbooks or when PMAX stops scaling.","steps":["PMAX has hit its ceiling: early discounts in the auction created arbitrage, then everyone moved spend in and the advantage went away. There's no clear visibility into where spend goes, and scaling PMAX to $100–300K/month did not produce matching backend revenue in the source's tests.","Standard shopping is back: once PMAX scales far enough it shows diminishing returns, and layering standard shopping is required to keep growing cold new-customer acquisition.","Match types changed: exact match now matches on meaning, phrase match broadened, broad match stayed broad. SCAGs (single-keyword ad groups) is no longer recommended — the source says it stopped working around 2020.","AIMAX and demand gen have been introduced; DSAs are being deprecated.","Structure the account around these realities rather than 2022–23 playbooks, and expect the platform to ship changes every few months."],"caveats":["This reflects the source's 2026 view; verify current platform behaviour and product availability before acting."],"tags":["multi","google-ads","pmax","campaign-structure","platform-changes","media-buying"]}]}
